claims.claim: Livingston describes A Song of Ice and Fire as medievalism, in which a modern work refashions particular elements of the Middle Ages into a new imaginative construction.
claims.source: Michael Livingston, "Getting Medieval on George R. R. Martin", Reactor/Tor.com (2015-07-16)
claims.quote: refashions particular elements of the Middle Ages into a new imaginative construction

claims.claim: Martin says a good editor tries to figure out what the writer was trying to do and helps him do it better rather than changing the book into something else.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, "Editors: The Writer's Natural Enemy", GoH speech, Coastcon II (1979-03-10)
claims.quote: tries to figure out what the writer was trying to do
claims.page: speech, section on what a good editor is like

claims.claim: Martin says a writer lives or dies by his words and must always have the last word if the work is to retain its integrity.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, "Editors: The Writer's Natural Enemy", GoH speech, Coastcon II (1979-03-10)
claims.quote: a writer lives or dies by his words
claims.page: speech, section on what a good editor is like

claims.claim: Martin condemns editors who make changes without bothering to inform the writer.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, "Editors: The Writer's Natural Enemy", GoH speech, Coastcon II (1979-03-10)
claims.quote: make the changes without bothering to inform the writer

claims.claim: Martin reports that editor Robert Hoskins rejected his story "With Morning Comes Mistfall" by calling it a travelog.
claims.source: Robert Hoskins, quoted in George R.R. Martin's Coastcon II speech (1979-03-10)

claims.claim: Martin reports that Hoskins returned one of his stories with a note saying it was eloquent but not a story.
claims.source: Robert Hoskins, quoted in George R.R. Martin's Coastcon II speech (1979-03-10)
claims.quote: it was “eloquent,” but not a story

claims.claim: Martin quotes editor Robert Hoskins telling him he had a facile way with words.
claims.source: Robert Hoskins, quoted in George R.R. Martin's Coastcon II speech (1979-03-10)
claims.quote: You have a facile way with words
claims.page: speech, Hoskins anecdote on "Night of the Vampyres"

claims.claim: Martin says Fire & Blood is a pseudo history of sorts by an in-world character rather than a traditional novel.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18, published 2022-08-25)
claims.quote: it is a pseudo history of sorts, by an in world character
claims.page: transcript, section on Fire & Blood and canon

claims.claim: Martin says he first called Fire & Blood fake history and switched to imaginary history after readers said they hated the first term.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: I called it fake history at first
claims.page: transcript, section on Fire & Blood and canon

claims.feature: other: competing versions in one record
claims.claim: Martin says he decided to give all versions of an event in Fire & Blood because history is uncertain.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: Why don’t I give all versions? Cause history is uncertain.

claims.claim: Martin says that in Fire & Blood, unlike a chapter of The Winds of Winter, he did not have to make up his mind about how an event happened.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: I didn’t have to have to make up my mind

claims.claim: Martin says researching the New York World building taught him that history is unreliable about what actually happened.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: it’s so unreliable to know what actually happened

claims.claim: Martin reports that his sources disagreed on how many stories the New York World building had, giving fourteen, fifteen and twenty.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: It had 15 stories. Now, wait a minute. This other book, 14.

claims.claim: Martin says he wanted to make the Nightfort a sinister place with its own legends.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: I did wanna make the Nightfort a sinister place, with its own legends
claims.page: transcript, section on homages and the Nightfort

claims.claim: Martin says that when he adapts something from history he never wants to make it smaller.
claims.source: George R.R. Martin, History of Westeros interview (recorded 2022-08-18)
claims.quote: you don’t ever wanna make it smaller
claims.page: transcript, section on turning history up
